questions.question: What does LRU stand for and what is the eviction policy?
options: Last Recently Updated — evict the last updated item
Least Recently Used — evict the item that hasn't been accessed for the longest time
Least Redundant Unit — evict duplicate items first
Last Read Update — evict based on the last read timestamp
questions.explanation: LRU stands for Least Recently Used. When the cache is full, it evicts the item that was accessed least recently. Any access — read or write — refreshes an item's position so it won't be evicted soon.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of GET and PUT operations in an optimally implemented LRU cache?
options: GET is O(1), PUT is O(n)
GET is O(log n), PUT is O(log n)
Both GET and PUT are O(1)
Both GET and PUT are O(n)
questions.explanation: With a hash map for O(1) lookups and a doubly-linked list for O(1) insertion/removal, both GET and PUT operations achieve O(1) time complexity. This is the key insight of the LRU cache design.

questions.question: Why is an array-based implementation of LRU cache considered suboptimal?
options: Arrays cannot store key-value pairs
Moving an accessed element to the front requires shifting all other elements, making it O(n)
Arrays have a fixed size and cannot support eviction
Arrays don't support random access
questions.explanation: When an item is accessed in an array, moving it to the front requires shifting all elements between its old and new position, which is O(n). A doubly-linked list avoids this by allowing O(1) node removal and insertion at the head.

questions.question: In the hash map + doubly-linked list design, what does the hash map store?
options: Key to value mappings only
Key to linked list node pointer mappings
Node pointers to key mappings
Key to array index mappings
questions.explanation: The hash map maps each key to a pointer/reference to its corresponding node in the doubly-linked list. This lets you jump directly to any node in O(1) without traversing the list, enabling O(1) removal and repositioning.

questions.question: Why must the linked list be doubly-linked rather than singly-linked?
options: Doubly-linked lists use less memory
Singly-linked lists don't support iteration
Removing a node from a singly-linked list requires finding its predecessor, which is O(n)
Doubly-linked lists are faster to traverse
questions.explanation: To remove a node from a linked list, you must update the previous node's next pointer. In a singly-linked list, finding the previous node requires O(n) traversal. A doubly-linked list stores a prev pointer, enabling O(1) removal from any position.

questions.question: During a PUT operation on a full LRU cache, which node is evicted and what happens in the hash map?
options: The head node is evicted; its hash map entry is updated
The tail node is evicted; its key is removed from the hash map
A random node is evicted; the hash map is rebuilt
The node with the smallest key is evicted; the hash map stays unchanged
questions.explanation: The tail node represents the least recently used item. It is removed from the list, and its key is deleted from the hash map. Then the new item is inserted at the head of the list and added to the hash map.

questions.question: How does Redis implement its LRU eviction policy differently from a textbook LRU cache?
options: Redis uses a B-tree instead of a linked list
Redis samples a random subset of keys and evicts the oldest among them (approximated LRU)
Redis implements exact LRU using a doubly-linked list
Redis doesn't support LRU eviction at all
questions.explanation: Redis uses approximated LRU to avoid the memory overhead of maintaining a doubly-linked list across millions of keys. It samples a configurable number of random keys and evicts the one with the oldest access timestamp. This is nearly as effective as exact LRU with far less overhead.

questions.question: A multi-threaded application uses an LRU cache with a global mutex. Under heavy concurrent reads, what is the primary performance bottleneck?
options: Hash collisions in the hash map
Memory allocation for new nodes
Lock contention — all reads serialize because every GET modifies the list ordering
Network latency between threads
questions.explanation: Unlike a typical read-heavy cache where reads don't mutate state, an LRU cache must move the accessed node to the head on every GET. This makes every read a write to the list, causing all operations to serialize under a global mutex, destroying concurrency.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of an LRU cache with capacity N?
options: O(1) — constant space regardless of capacity
O(N) — the hash map and linked list each store N entries
O(N log N) — due to the hash map's internal tree structure
O(N^2) — due to the doubly-linked list's bidirectional pointers
questions.explanation: The hash map stores N key-to-node mappings and the doubly-linked list stores N nodes, each with prev/next pointers and a key-value pair. Total space is O(N) + O(N) = O(N). The extra pointer overhead per node is constant.

questions.question: You're designing an LRU cache where some items should never be evicted (pinned items). How do you modify the design?
options: Increase the cache capacity to infinity so eviction never happens
Store pinned items in a separate section of the list that the eviction logic skips, and adjust effective capacity accordingly
Remove the eviction logic entirely
Use a different cache replacement policy like FIFO
questions.explanation: Pinned items can be stored outside the evictable portion of the list, or flagged so the eviction scan skips them. The effective capacity for evictable items becomes (total capacity - pinned count). This keeps O(1) operations while supporting pinning.
